claims.claim: In September 1955, A.A. Rayner & Sons (4141 S. Cottage Grove, Chicago) received Emmett Till's sealed casket from Mississippi on September 2, opened it at Mamie Till-Mobley's insistence, prepared the body for public viewing under glass, and hosted visitation; the funeral was held at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ on September 3, 1955, and burial followed at Burr Oak Cemetery on September 6, 1955.
claims.evidence: Landmark report records funeral arrangements with A.A. Rayner & Sons; remains arrived Sept 2, 1955; Till-Mobley pressured A.A. Rayner Jr. to open the sealed container; body prepared for public viewing with glass cover; tens of thousands viewed at Rayner and Roberts Temple; burial at Burr Oak Sept 6, 1955.
claims.notes: Crowd counts vary (see C-02). Mamie Till-Mobley's agency is central; the funeral home supplied professional/physical machinery.
claims.source: City of Chicago, Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley House landmark designation report

claims.claim: Approximately 50,000 people viewed Emmett Till's body at A.A. Rayner & Sons; 100,000 attended across the viewing and funeral days.
claims.contradictory_evidence: The two figures measure different scopes (single venue vs. all venues/days) but are routinely quoted as conflicting totals.
claims.evidence: Till Memory Project: ~50,000 at Rayner viewing. Duckworth office: 100,000 across viewing/funeral days.
claims.notes: Preserve variance; do not cite a single number.
claims.source: Emmett Till Memory Project (50,000 at Rayner); Office of Sen. Tammy Duckworth (100,000 across venues/days)

claims.claim: On July 25, 2023, President Biden designated the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument, including Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ in Chicago (site of the 1955 open-casket visitation and funeral), Graball Landing, and the Tallahatchie County Courthouse.
claims.evidence: NPS release: designation July 25, 2023; three sites; Roberts Temple described as site of widely attended open casket visitation and funeral.
claims.source: National Park Service news release, Aug 29, 2023

claims.claim: Undertaker Clarie Collins Harvey of Jackson, Mississippi, used her funeral home's vehicles, business networks, meeting space, and economic independence to support Freedom Riders (May 1961), fund Womanpower Unlimited, distribute movement information, and host civil-rights strategy sessions.
claims.evidence: Article grounded in Clarie Collins Harvey Papers, Amistad Research Center (1981 oral history; Womanpower Unlimited records).
claims.notes: National comparison case; does not prove identical functions in Chicago.
claims.source: Crystal R. Sanders, 'Dignity in Life and Death: Undertaker Clarie Collins Harvey and Black Women's Entrepreneurial Activism,' Journal of Mississippi History (Fall/Winter 2014)

claims.claim: Black funeral homes nationally supplied meeting space for movement organizing, voter-registration equipment (tables, chairs, tents), bail assistance, transportation, scholarships, and community facilities (gospel singings, church services, music lessons); funeral directors acted as informal lenders and information hubs.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Synthetic survey; some claims rest on single interviews or cited secondary work rather than archival records.
claims.evidence: Survey article synthesizing industry sources, funeral-director interviews, and secondary literature; specific examples: Poole Funeral Chapels (Birmingham), J.F. Bell Funeral Home (Charlottesville), Black funeral directors as 'casual lenders.'
claims.notes: DOI 10.3390/rel11080390. Author: Candi K. Cann, Baylor University.
claims.source: Candi K. Cann, 'Black Deaths Matter: Earning the Right to Live — Death and the African-American Funeral Home,' Religions 11(8):390 (2020)

claims.claim: Chicago Black funeral homes routinely hosted political meetings and movement strategy sessions in their halls.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Absence of located evidence is not evidence of absence.
claims.evidence: Same assets and segregated conditions as documented national cases; Till case proves capacity for mass political witness. No archival record of a specific Chicago meeting located.
claims.notes: Largest Chicago-specific evidence gap; priority for oral-history research.
claims.source: Structural inference from C-04/C-05; no Chicago-specific archival source located

claims.claim: Black funeral-home founders operated 'without access to traditional credit markets,' making the firms family affairs that at times branched into real estate and transportation.
claims.evidence: Business Reference Librarian, Science Technology & Business Division, summarizing industry history.
claims.notes: Institutional blog, not a research publication; graded SUPPORTED not VERIFIED.
claims.source: Lynn Weinstein, 'Honoring African Americans: Celebrating Life in Death – African American Funeral Homes,' Library of Congress Inside Adams blog (Feb 2021)

claims.claim: Black funeral directors functioned as informal neighborhood lenders ('casual lenders') — small loans, bill-paying, informal banking.
claims.evidence: Survey reports interview testimony; no ledgers or loan records cited.
claims.notes: Plausible given credit exclusion; not documented with financial records.
claims.source: Cann (2020), citing funeral-director interviews and industry sources

claims.claim: Leak & Sons was founded to provide dignified burial for Black Chicagoans lacking alternatives, and worked with families regardless of means.
claims.evidence: Family/press accounts of 1933 founding by Rev. A.R. Leak with World's Fair savings and a loan from his wife Dottie.
claims.notes: Founding-capital details are family testimony, not corporate records.
claims.source: Leak & Sons company history; Chicago Sun-Times-derived reporting (usanewssite.com, 2026)

claims.claim: Black burial societies pooled dues to pay for funerals, sickness aid, and widow/child support; the Free African Society (Philadelphia, 1787, founded by Richard Allen and Absalom Jones) began the lineage; Du Bois (1899) counted 100 societies with 7,448 members by 1838, $18,851 paid in, $14,171 in benefits paid.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Cann's article once gives '1778' for the Free African Society — an internal inconsistency; 1787 is used here per consensus.
claims.evidence: Du Bois's 1899 accounting figures; Free African Society founding 1787 is standard historical consensus.
claims.notes: See red team on the 1778/1787 discrepancy.
claims.source: W.E.B. Du Bois, The Philadelphia Negro (1899); Cann (2020) summarizing

claims.claim: In the Till case, A.A. Rayner & Sons functioned as an information-network node where a grieving family, the Black press, and a mass public converged — demonstrating the funeral director's structural position as a neighborhood information hub.
claims.evidence: Press coverage of the viewing at Rayner; photographs published in Jet; national attention converging on the funeral home.
claims.notes: Demonstrates capacity, not routine practice.
claims.source: City of Chicago landmark report; Facing History & Ourselves; OUPblog (Dave Tell)

claims.claim: Funeral parlors 'operate by reputation and word of mouth and are built around relationships'; funeral directors were 'often leaders in their community' and 'a base of operation within a neighborhood'; Black funeral entrepreneurs 'often became leadership figures in their communities.'
claims.evidence: Direct quotations from LOC business-reference post.
claims.source: Lynn Weinstein, Library of Congress Inside Adams blog (Feb 2021)

claims.claim: Chicago funeral directors systematically relayed movement intelligence (strategy, boycott information) to civil-rights organizers.
claims.evidence: Documented for Harvey in Mississippi; not documented for any Chicago director.
claims.notes: Do not generalize the Harvey case to Chicago without evidence.
claims.source: Harvey case (Sanders 2014) as national precedent; no Chicago documentation located

claims.claim: Named Chicago funeral directors trained at Worsham College: A.A. Rayner Sr. studied there before founding his firm (1947); Ernest A. Griffin graduated from Worsham in 1934; Spencer Leak Jr. earned a mortuary science degree from Southern Illinois University (1989).
claims.evidence: Worsham founding (March 17, 1911, Albert Worsham) confirmed by Illinois Board of Higher Education records.
claims.notes: Worsham was NOT Black-owned — see red team.
claims.source: Rayner company 'About Us' page; Congressional Record Vol. 141 (Griffin tribute, Dec 18, 1995); Sun-Times-derived reporting on Spencer Leak Jr.

claims.claim: Women's labor was central to Chicago funeral firms: Alyce Louise Carter Griffin was a licensed funeral director and embalmer who worked in the family business from 1958 and ran it after her husband's 1995 death; Dottie Leak's loan capitalized Leak & Sons' founding; Rayner family histories credit the founder's children with building the business.
claims.evidence: Obituary: licensed director/embalmer, worked from 1958, ran firm after 1995. Leak: $500 loan from wife Dottie (family account).
claims.notes: Women's ownership/labor remains under-documented overall.
claims.source: Chicago Sun-Times obituary (Alyce Griffin, via Legacy, 2017); Sun-Times-derived reporting on Leak; Rayner company history

claims.claim: Funeral programs preserve birth/death dates, family names, church and organizational offices, service order, pallbearers, and interment locations — a biographical archive for Black genealogy; NMAAHC holds funeral programs as collection objects.
claims.evidence: Catalog entry documents program contents; Essence documents genealogical use.
claims.notes: No Chicago-specific funeral-program archive located.
claims.source: NMAAHC catalog (nmaahc_2014.117.71, 1990 funeral program); Essence reporting (Bridgette deGregory) on funeral programs in Black genealogy

claims.claim: The business records of A.A. Rayner & Sons, Leak & Sons, and Griffin Funeral Home are held in a publicly accessible archive.
claims.evidence: No repository identified for any of the three firms' papers; Griffin closed 2007; Rayner and Leak archives not publicly located.
claims.notes: Sharpest records gap; priority next research step.
claims.source: None located

claims.claim: Griffin Funeral Home erected a Heritage Memorial Wall in 1990 honoring the founder's Civil War veteran grandfather and the Camp Douglas history of the Bronzeville site — a funeral home performing public memory work.
claims.evidence: Newberry documents the wall, the founder, and the site's Camp Douglas connection.
claims.source: Newberry Library blog, 'A Chicago Funeral Home and Civil War Site'

claims.claim: In 2016 the U.S. funeral industry generated ~$14.2 billion in annual revenue from 15,818 funeral homes; ~1,200 were family-owned African American independent businesses; four publicly traded consolidators absorb family firms where succession fails or credit gaps bite.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; underlying industry dataset not independently verified.
claims.evidence: As reported in LOC post.
claims.notes: National figures; no Chicago breakdown.
claims.source: Lynn Weinstein, Library of Congress Inside Adams blog (Feb 2021), citing industry data

claims.claim: Corporate consolidators targeted the ~4,000 mostly family-owned Black funeral homes, drawn by high Black mortality rates and a strong preference for traditional burial over cremation.
claims.evidence: As reported in Cann's survey.
claims.notes: Framing ('targeted') is the Journal's; treat as reported, not independently verified.
claims.source: Cann (2020), citing The Wall Street Journal

claims.claim: Chicago-specific funeral-sector economics are known: market share, pricing, consolidation acquisitions, and cremation trends among Black funeral homes.
claims.evidence: No verified data located for this brief.
claims.notes: Explicitly deferred to CTL-DR-ECON-001.
claims.source: None located

claims.claim: The Metropolitan Funeral Home building at 4445 S. King Dr became the Chicago Defender's headquarters in May 2009 — a funeral-home building repurposed as Black press infrastructure.
claims.evidence: Editor & Publisher reporting via CTL-DR-BIZ-000001 research; move announced May 2009.
claims.notes: Single secondary source; cross-referenced from sibling package.
claims.source: Editor & Publisher (2009), via CTL-DR-BIZ-000001

claims.claim: Johnson Publishing Company's offices at 1820 S. Michigan Ave (1949–1971) occupied a former funeral home.
claims.evidence: Single secondary source in sibling research.
claims.notes: Needs corroboration before narrative use.
claims.source: CTL-DR-BIZ-000001 research notes (single secondary)

claims.claim: Ernest A. Griffin (Congressional Record spells 'Earnest Griffin') graduated Worsham College of Mortuary Science in 1934, purchased Bell Auto & Undertaking Co. in 1947, moved it to 3232 S. King Dr in 1969, conducted final rites for Elijah Muhammad and Jesse Owens, was the first African American invited into an international thanatology association, served 20+ years on Lakeside Bank's board, and received a Congressional Record tribute (Dec 18, 1995). The firm closed December 31, 2007.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record Vol. 141, Issue 203 (Extensions of Remarks); Newberry Library blog; Alyce Griffin obituary (Chicago Sun-Times via Legacy, Feb 2017) for closure date.
claims.notes: Use 'Ernest A. Griffin' as working form with spelling note. Closure date rests on obituary single-source; flag accordingly.
claims.source: Congressional Record; Newberry Library blog; Chicago Sun-Times obituary (Alyce Griffin)

claims.claim: Leak & Sons Funeral Homes was founded in 1933 by Rev. Andrew 'A.R.' Leak and continues operating (flagship 7838 S. Cottage Grove Ave, Chicago); the firm handled funerals for Sam Cooke (1964) and Rev. Jesse L. Jackson Sr. (2026); Spencer Leak Jr. (third generation, d. May 2026) was its public face.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on founding year or continuity.
claims.evidence: Company history; Sun-Times-derived 2026 reporting; Black Enterprise (June 1, 2026) lists notable funerals (Sam Cooke 1964, Bernie Mac, Juice WRLD, Jesse Jackson Sr. 2026).
claims.notes: Founding-capital details ($500 loan, World's Fair savings) are family/press accounts — graded within C-09.
claims.source: Leak & Sons company history; Chicago Sun-Times-derived reporting; Black Enterprise

claims.claim: Ahmed A. Rayner Sr. founded A.A. Rayner & Sons in 1947 at 4141 S. Cottage Grove after mortuary training (Worsham, Prairie View A&M) and employment at Jackson Funeral Home and as livery manager at Metropolitan Funeral Home (affiliated with Chicago Metropolitan Mutual Life Assurance Co.).
claims.evidence: Company self-history; trademark record (first use Jan 1, 1947) consistent with founding year.
claims.notes: Institutional self-history; corroborate founding details before elevation to VERIFIED.
claims.source: aaraynerandsonsfuneralhome.com/about-us/; USPTO trademark registration (first use Jan 1, 1947)

claims.claim: Burr Oak Cemetery was founded in 1927 in Alsip, Illinois as a Black-owned and managed cemetery; Emmett Till was buried there September 6, 1955 with a fifty-car procession; the Illinois Historic Sites Advisory Council recommended it for the National Register in 2025.
claims.evidence: Till Memory Project (founding 1927; burial Sept 6, 1955; 50-car procession); City landmark report (burial); 2025 NR recommendation (AfroConsciousMedia/press).
claims.notes: Also burial site of Dinah Washington, Ezzard Charles, Willie Dixon, Roberta Martin, Earl B. Dickerson, Annie Malone, Rev. Clay Evans.
claims.source: Emmett Till Memory Project; City of Chicago landmark report; press (2025)

claims.claim: In July 2009, Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart announced that four Burr Oak Cemetery workers were accused of digging up graves and reselling burial plots.
claims.evidence: AP and Chicago Tribune reporting on the sheriff's announcement.
claims.notes: Included as counter-evidence: institutional vulnerability, not celebration.
claims.source: Associated Press; Chicago Tribune (July 2009)
